1.3 Mapping animae

The mapping animae will play an important role in the development of the theory: frequently, we may check conditions at the level of mapping animae. We introduce them by evaluation and a universal property with anima parameters.

Axiom B.1 (Evaluation and currying for mapping animae). Agda For categories \(C,D\), there is an anima \(\Map (C,D)\) equipped with an evaluation functor \[ \ev _{\Map }\colon \Map (C,D)\times C\longrightarrow D. \] If \(X\) is an anima and \(h:X\times C\to D\) is a functor, there is a functor \(h_c\colon X\to \Map (C,D)\) equipped with a natural isomorphism \((h_c)^u\cong h\), where \[ a^u:=\ev _{\Map }\circ (a\times \id _C):X\times C\longrightarrow D. \] For any \(a,b\colon X\to \Map (C,D)\), the functor \[ (-)^u\colon (a\cong b)\longrightarrow (a^u\cong b^u) \] induced by product functoriality and postwhiskering with evaluation is an equivalence.

Construction 1.3.1 (Functors as points of mapping animae). A functor \(f\colon C\to D\) determines a point \(\ulcorner f\urcorner \colon *\to \Map (C,D)\) by currying \(f\pr _2\colon *\times C\to D\). Conversely, a point \(a:*\to \Map (C,D)\) determines the functor \[ C\simeq *\times C\xrightarrow {a\times \id _C}\Map (C,D)\times C \xrightarrow {\ev _{\Map }}D. \] Beta and the product unitor identify the functor represented by \(\ulcorner f\urcorner \) with \(f\). Moreover, for two points \(a,b\), uncurrying followed by prewhiskering with \(C\simeq *\times C\) gives an equivalence from \((a\cong b)\) to the isomorphism anima between their represented functors. Here we use Lemma 1.2.11. This equivalence also identifies a point with the representative of its represented functor.

decode-name

decode-name : {C D : CAT} (f : MAP C D) → =₁ (decodeMap (nameMap f)) f

      (mapCurry-β one-isAn (f ∘ pr₂) ▷ oneProduct-in C)))

decodeMap-isoMap-isEquiv

Derivation, checked

decodeMap-isoMap-isEquiv : {C D : CAT} (a b : Obj-abs (Map C D))

Proof / implementation
decodeMap-isoMap-isEquiv {C} a b =

    (mapUncurry-isoMap-isEquiv one-isAn a b)

name-decode

Derivation, checked

name-decode : {C D : CAT} (a : Obj-abs (Map C D)) → =₁ (nameMap (decodeMap a)) a
Proof / implementation
name-decode {C} a = mapReflect one-isAn _ a
  (comp-unitʳ (mapUncurry a) ∙
    ((mapUncurry a ◁ oneProduct-section C) ∙
      (comp-assoc pr₂ (oneProduct-in C) (mapUncurry a) ∙
        mapCurry-β one-isAn (decodeMap a ∘ pr₂))))

We will usually denote the point \(\ulcorner f\urcorner \) simply by \(f\). Passing between a functor and its representing point uses the comparisons just described.

Lemma 1.3.2 (Specialization). A functor \(H:\Map (A,B)\to \Map (C,D)\) acts on a functor \(f\colon A\to B\) by applying \(H\) to its representing point and interpreting the result as a functor \(C\to D\). We denote it by \(H(f)\). This operation preserves identity functors and composition of the functors \(H\) through the representing comparisons. It also acts on natural isomorphisms and their identifications. If \(H\) is an equivalence, it lifts and reflects those natural isomorphisms and identifications.

Agda Lifting and reflection through specialization

specializeMap-isoMap-isEquiv

Derivation, checked

specializeMap-isoMap-isEquiv : {A B C D : CAT} (H : MAP (Map A B) (Map C D))
  → IsEquiv H → (f g : MAP A B) → IsEquiv (specializeMap-isoMap H f g)
Proof / implementation
specializeMap-isoMap-isEquiv H e f g =
  equiv-compose (postWhisker H ∘ nameMap-isoMap f g)
    (decodeMap-isoMap (H ∘ nameMap f) (H ∘ nameMap g))
    (equiv-compose (nameMap-isoMap f g) (postWhisker H)
      (nameMap-isoMap-isEquiv f g) (postWhisker-isEquiv H e (nameMap f) (nameMap g)))

Construction 1.3.4. The mapping animae are covariantly functorial in the second variable and contravariantly functorial in the first. For \(g\colon D\to E\), curry the composite \[ \Map (C,D)\times C\xrightarrow {\ev _{\Map }}D\xrightarrow {g}E \] to obtain \(g_*\colon \Map (C,D)\to \Map (C,E)\). For \(f\colon B\to C\), curry evaluation precomposed with \(\id _{\Map (C,D)}\times f\) to obtain \(f^*\colon \Map (C,D)\to \Map (B,D)\). We call these functors postcomposition with \(g\) and precomposition with \(f\), respectively.

A natural isomorphism \(\gamma \colon g\cong g'\) induces a natural isomorphism \(\gamma _*\colon g_*\cong g'_*\). Indeed, whisker \(\gamma \) with evaluation and use the uncurrying comparisons for \(g_*\) and \(g'_*\) to obtain an isomorphism between their uncurried functors. Lift this through the equivalence of isomorphism animae in the mapping-anima rule. Similarly, for \(\varphi \colon f\cong f'\), pair \(\varphi \) with the identity on \(\Map (C,D)\), postcompose with evaluation, and lift to obtain \(\varphi ^*\colon f^*\cong f'^*\).

Proof

Proof. Expand uncurrying as evaluation after the product functor \(f\times \id _C\). The first comparison is the composite of the associator for functor composition with the comparison \[ (f\circ \sigma )\times \id _C \cong (f\times \id _C)\circ (\sigma \times \id _C) \] from functoriality of products. Naturality in both variables follows by applying horizontal composition and the corresponding comparison for products. The identity, vertical composition, whiskering, and iterated-precomposition statements follow from Axioms A.5 to A.7 and Lemma 1.2.20. These are precisely the finite comparisons used below. □

1.3.1 Composition and application

Construction 1.3.7 (Composition and identity). For categories \(C,D,E\), double evaluation gives a functor \[ \Map (D,E)\times \Map (C,D)\times C\longrightarrow E, \] which first evaluates the second functor at the \(C\)-variable and then evaluates the first functor at the resulting \(D\)-variable. Currying in \(C\) constructs a functor \[ \mu _{C,D,E}\colon \Map (D,E)\times \Map (C,D)\longrightarrow \Map (C,E). \] Its beta isomorphism is the universal comparison \[ \ev _{\Map }\bigl (\mu (g,f),c\bigr ) \cong \ev _{\Map }\bigl (g,\ev _{\Map }(f,c)\bigr ). \tag{1.5}\]Agda

Proof

Proof. Compare the two routes by their projections. On the parameter factor, use the projection comparisons. On the other factor, expand the chosen evaluation comparisons and use Lemma 1.3.6; interchange moves a comparison through the next evaluation. The product universal property lifts these identifications, with their prescribed projections. The identity case uses the identity evaluation comparison and the unit laws. The same projection argument compares threefold composition and composition with the identity: their second projections are the primitive pentagon and triangle, respectively. □

Construction 1.3.9 (Associator and unitors). For three composable functor variables, take \(P\) to be the product of the three mapping animae. The evaluation of either parenthesized composite is compared, using the chosen evaluation comparisons, with the corresponding composite of the three functors which retain \(P\) and evaluate one variable. Define the associator by transporting the primitive associator through these two comparisons and lifting through the isomorphism-anima equivalence for uncurrying. Define the unitors in the same way, using the evaluation comparison for the point representing an identity functor. Denote these comparisons by \(\alpha _{f,g,h}\), \(\lambda _f\), and \(\rho _f\), as for primitive composition.

Proof

Proof.

Now take \(P\) to be the product of four mapping animae. At each of the five parenthesizations, expand the two or three occurrences of mapping composition using the chosen evaluation comparisons. Keep the resulting comparison with the corresponding parenthesized composite of the four parameter-retaining functors fixed. There are five edges to check. The edges from \(((kh)g)f\) to \((k(hg))f\) and from \(k((hg)f)\) to \(k(h(gf))\) apply the three-variable associator inside a larger expression; their evaluations use interchange to move its evaluation comparison through the remaining composition. The other three edges use the associator on the triples \((kh,g,f)\), \((k,h,gf)\) and \((k,hg,f)\). For each of these, first apply the evaluation comparison for the displayed two-variable composite, and then use naturality of the primitive associator with respect to that comparison. In every case the evaluated edge is thereby identified with the primitive edge, preceded by the fixed comparison at its source and followed by the inverse of the fixed comparison at its target. The parameter-retaining comparisons have the same identification by Lemmas 1.3.8 and 1.3.10.

Composing along either side of the pentagon now cancels the intermediate comparisons by the unit and inverse laws for natural isomorphisms. Both composites have the same outside comparisons, and the primitive pentagon identifies the two remaining composites. The isomorphism-anima equivalence for uncurrying reflects this identification and gives the desired pentagon. For the triangle, use the product of two mapping animae as parameter and expand the occurrence of the representing identity by its evaluation comparison. The parameter-retaining identity is identified with the identity of \(P\times C\) by the product universal property. Naturality moves this comparison past the associator, after which the two evaluated paths have the same outside comparisons and are identified by the primitive triangle. Reflection through uncurrying gives the triangle for mapping composition. Restricting each whole identity along a functor from any categorical parameter gives its contextual instance, retaining the indicated endpoint comparisons. □

    (g : MAP P (Map B C)) (f : MAP P (Map A B))
    → Pentagon.Statement k h g f
Proof / implementation

    (universal-assoc pAn (composeTerm k h) g f)

    (universal-assoc pAn k h g)
    (universal-assoc pAn k (composeTerm h g) f)
    (universal-assoc pAn h g f)

Proof

Proof. We prove (i) \(\Leftrightarrow \) (ii); the other case is dual. An inverse of \(f\) induces an inverse of every \(f_*\). Conversely, choose an inverse \(H\colon \Map (D,D)\to \Map (D,C)\) of \(f_*\colon \Map (D,C)\to \Map (D,D)\). Specialization of \(H\) at \(\id _D\) gives a functor \(g\colon D\to C\). The unit of the equivalence and the beta comparison for postcomposition give \(f\circ g\cong \id _D\).

Proof

Proof. The inverse of the product unitor, followed by evaluation, gives a functor \(\Map (*,A)\to A\). The beta comparison identifies one composite with the identity. After uncurrying, it also identifies the other composite with the identity; the lifting clause then provides the second inverse isomorphism. □

Agda The two comparisons for absolute objects

backward-forward

Derivation, checked

  backward-forward : =₁ (backward ∘ forward) (id A)
Proof / implementation
  backward-forward = pair-β₁ (id A) (terminate A) ∙
    ((forward-β ▷ product-unit-inverse A) ∙
    (invIso (comp-assoc (product-unit-inverse A) (productMap forward (id One)) mapEval) ∙
    ((mapEval ◁ invIso (insert-terminal-natural forward)) ∙
      comp-assoc forward (product-unit-inverse (Map One A)) mapEval)))
